row.note: Exodus says God led the redeemed people by strength to his holy abode; it supplies a scriptural journey whose end is a dwelling, the completion the commentary hears in ihdinā.
The psalm asks that God's light and truth lead the speaker and bring him to God's holy hill and dwellings, closely joining guidance with arrival at a sacred home.
God leads wilderness wanderers by a straight way until they reach a city to inhabit; the verse makes a straight road culminate in a place of belonging.
God sends an angel to guard Israel on the way and bring them to a prepared place, combining escort, safety, and a divinely assigned destination.
Nations go up to the house of Jacob's God so that he may teach them his ways and they may walk his paths; house and guided way are one scene.
Abraham is told to go to Moriah and offer on a mountain God will show him, a sacrifice directed toward a disclosed destination rather than offered anywhere.
The ram caught at Moriah is offered in Isaac's place, giving the selected mountain an actual animal offering within the Akedah scene.
Chronicles places Solomon's Temple on Mount Moriah, canonically joining the shown sacrificial mountain to the later house of worship.
God calls the chosen Temple site a house of sacrifice, an unusually direct biblical pairing of house and sacrificial destination.
An ox, lamb, or goat slaughtered for sacrifice must be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting before YHWH; the animal's holy use depends on reaching the appointed place.
Israel must bring its offerings to the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, directly linking name, sacred house, and transported sacrifices.
The Passover sacrifice is taken from flock or herd and offered at the place YHWH chooses for his name to dwell, closely matching animal, house, and named worship.
God brings foreign adherents to his holy mountain; their offerings are accepted on his altar in a house of prayer, bringing outsider reception and sacrifice together.
Camels carry gold and frankincense to Zion while proclaiming YHWH's praise, a caravan image that joins the commentary's camels, carried gift, and exalted name.

row.basis: flocks on altar and glorified house
row.note: Flocks are accepted on God's altar and he glorifies his house; this makes herd animals reach the sanctuary for worship.
A gift or tribute is brought to the place of the name of YHWH on Zion, giving a biblical destination for a carried offering.

row.basis: male from flock and great Name
row.note: Malachi contrasts a vowed male animal withheld from sacrifice with YHWH's great name among nations, directly coupling flock, offering, and name.
The worshiper offers a thanksgiving sacrifice and calls on YHWH's name, an explicit analogue to sacrifice accompanied by divine naming.
The prophetic vision of incense and a pure offering for YHWH's great name gives the name-and-offering conjunction developed in the commentary.
The Passover sacrifice belongs to YHWH who passed over Israelite houses; sacrifice, named worship, household, and protection meet in one rite.
Rebekah and her attendants mount camels and follow Abraham's servant, beginning a bridal journey with the animal explicitly named in the commentary.
Isaac brings Rebekah into Sarah's tent and takes her as wife; the bridal journey ends in incorporation into the husband's household.
God forms the woman and brings her to the man, a concise biblical scene of a bride being led to her husband.
Laban brings Leah to Jacob at night; the same transfer scene appears here within a deceptive marriage narrative, which keeps the relation from being idealized.
Esther is taken to the king in his royal palace, a courtly version of a woman being conveyed into a husband's household.
Boaz says that he has acquired Ruth as wife; it is a biblical legal idiom in which marriage is expressed through acquisition, relevant to the commentary's imlāk image.
God covers Jerusalem, swears an oath, enters covenant, and says she became his; the prophetic marriage image makes covenant the act that establishes belonging.
The servant gives Rebekah ornaments and gives precious things to her kin, a gift-bearing scene embedded in the transfer of a bride.
The Queen of Sheba herself comes to Solomon with a camel caravan and wealth, whereas the Qur'anic scene developed in the commentary has the queen send a gift before meeting him.
The queen gives Solomon gold, spices, and precious stones; Kings narrates the transfer without Solomon's Qur'anic rebuff of the gift.
Kings has Solomon give the queen all she desired in addition to royal gifts, making reciprocal exchange rather than rejection the outcome of the parallel royal encounter.
God says he will not accept an offering from the speakers' hand; it supplies a different reason for an offered gift to fail to reach its intended acceptance.
At the three annual appearances before God, no one is to appear empty-handed; seasonal gathering, journey to the chosen place, and carried gift form one obligation.
Each pilgrim gives according to the blessing YHWH has given, a concrete biblical joining of gift, pilgrimage, and received benefit.
The mo'adim are YHWH's appointed times and holy convocations, a calendrical gathering marked out in a way comparable to the commentary's season-sign.
God appoints a place to which an accidental killer may flee, a foundational legal scene of flight toward secured space.
Israel designates cities of refuge so that a manslayer may flee there; refuge is reached by travel to a named communal place.
The refuge cities are for Israelites, resident aliens, and sojourners, making protected arrival available across communal status.

row.basis: admission and a place to dwell
row.note: A fugitive reaches the city gate, states his case to elders, is admitted, and receives a place to live among them; this is especially close to the commentary's seeker of protection.
The community may not hand an escaped slave back to his master, a direct rule against returning a person who has sought safety.
The escaped slave may live among the community in the place he chooses and must not be oppressed; protection is completed by a chosen home.
The appeal asks Judah to provide shade like night and hide the outcasts, a vivid shelter image for endangered arrivals.
The speaker asks that Moab's outcasts live with Judah and that Judah be a shelter from the destroyer, closely matching asylum in another community.
Adonijah fears Solomon and takes hold of the altar's horns, using sacred space and its object as a claim to protection.

row.basis: altar refuge has a legal limit
row.note: Exodus orders a presumptuous murderer taken even from God's altar; against the commentary's inviolable protected person, this marks the Torah's stated limit on sanctuary asylum.
Joshua makes peace with the Gibeonites, makes a covenant, and leaders swear to them; a community's word creates their protected status.
The leaders say the sworn oath prevents the congregation from striking the Gibeonites, showing the protective force of a covenantal promise.

row.basis: protective sign on a vulnerable person
row.note: God puts a sign on Cain so that no one who finds him will kill him; it is a marked person's inviolability, though not an asylum treaty.
Blood serves as a sign on Israelite houses and causes the plague to pass over; a mark makes a dwelling and those inside it inviolable.
God brings scattered people to dwell in Jerusalem, and they become his people while he becomes their God in faithfulness; arrival and covenantal belonging are inseparable.
Midrash on the Akedah identifies Moriah with the later sanctuary, reading Abraham's sacrificial journey as oriented toward the place that becomes God's house.
Pesahim contrasts Abraham's mountain and Isaac's field with Jacob's name for the future sanctuary as a house, sharpening the commentary's claim that sacred approach ends at a home.
The Mishnah makes appearance at the pilgrimage festivals an obligation with an offering, preserving the gathered-season and carried-sacrifice pattern as law.
The first-fruit towns assemble and ascend toward Zion in procession; it is a Jewish ritual realization of a marked gathering traveling with gifts to God's place.
The Mishnah describes first fruits borne in baskets and handed to priests, a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's carried gift and its tray.
The Mishnah says that after Jerusalem was chosen, high places were forbidden permanently; it interprets sacrifice as bound to its final house.
The midrash depicts God as acting as Adam's bridal attendant when he brings Eve to him, explicitly elaborating Genesis's bride-transfer scene.
The Mishnah opens by saying that a woman is acquired in three ways; it gives a Jewish legal frame for the commentary's marriage language in the malik family.
High priests' mothers supply food and clothing to accidental killers in refuge cities, treating arrival at refuge as an ongoing protected residence.
The Mishnah describes roads marked 'refuge, refuge' toward the cities of refuge; it makes the road itself visibly direct a fleeing person toward safety.
The star goes ahead of the magi until it stands over the place of the child, a guided journey that has a precise domestic destination.
The magi enter a house, worship the child, and open their treasures; destination, reverence, and a carried gift converge without requiring the gift to be a sacrifice.
Mary and Joseph bring Jesus to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord, a New Testament movement of a person toward the holy place for cultic presentation.
The couple offers the prescribed birds at the Temple; this supplies the animal-offering side of the Jerusalem presentation scene.
Those judged righteous say they gathered in a stranger; the concrete act of receiving an outsider gives a Christian household analogue to the protected arrival.
The Samaritan puts the wounded man on his own animal, brings him to an inn, and cares for him, a notably close scene of transport into safety.
Jesus describes his Father's house as having many dwelling places, giving the prayer for guidance an explicitly eschatological house as destination.
Jesus promises to come again and take his followers to himself so that they may be where he is, turning destination into belonging with a person.
Jesus calls himself the way to the Father; the Christian text personalizes the path whose end is the Father's house in the same discourse.

row.basis: betrothed and presented to one husband
row.note: Paul says he betrothed the community to one husband in order to present it as a pure virgin to Christ, directly recasting bride-transfer in ecclesial terms.
Ephesians names Gentiles as aliens from Israel and strangers to the covenants; it gives the exclusion from which the commentary's asylum-and-covenant image moves.
Those once strangers and aliens become fellow citizens and members of God's household, an unusually direct Christian counterpart to secure communal belonging.
Christ presents the church to himself in splendor; the marital image supplies the end-point of a bride brought to her husband.
Believers present their bodies as a living sacrifice, which Paul calls worship; it explicitly joins sacrifice with the service dimension the commentary draws from عبادت.
God highly exalts Jesus and grants the name above every name after the obedient self-giving of the preceding verse, a close Christian analogue to raised name and obedient service.
Paul calls the Philippians' material gift a fragrant, acceptable sacrifice pleasing to God, combining an affectional gift with sacrificial language.

row.basis: entry into holy place through sacrifice
row.note: Believers have confidence to enter the holy places by Jesus' blood; sacrifice here grants access to the sacred destination.
The access of the preceding verse is described as a new and living way, explicitly making sacrificial approach a path.

row.basis: sacrifice of praise and confession of Name
row.note: Through Jesus believers offer continual praise to God, identified as lips confessing his name; name and sacrifice are made verbal rather than animal.
Believers are built into a spiritual house and holy priesthood to offer spiritual sacrifices, fusing house, communal belonging, and worship.
Revelation's Lamb shepherds and guides people to springs of living water; it reverses the commentary's guided sacrificial animal into an animal figure that guides others.
The marriage of the Lamb comes and his bride has made herself ready, a final wedding scene that gives the bridal route an eschatological destination.
New Jerusalem descends prepared as a bride adorned for her husband; city-home and bride are deliberately merged in one arrival image.
The divine dwelling is among human beings and they are God's people, providing the final communal home sought in the commentary's road image.

row.basis: glory and honor brought into the city
row.note: The glory and honor of nations are brought into New Jerusalem, an eschatological analogue to gifts conveyed into the sacred home.
The victor becomes a permanent pillar in God's temple and bears God's name and the name of the new Jerusalem, combining inviolability, house, and name.
The Didache directs the community to gather, give thanks, and make its sacrifice pure; it is an early Christian liturgical continuation of gathered worship and offering.
Justin identifies Malachi's pure offering with Christian Eucharistic bread and cup, changing the prophetic name-and-offering text into a communal Christian rite.

row.basis: Arabic ع ب د and Hebrew עבד
row.note: The commentary's ع ب د label and Hebrew עבד are cognate service terms; Exodus has Israel serve God on the mountain after deliverance, without importing the commentary's camel sense into Hebrew.
Joshua's 'my house will serve YHWH' uses Hebrew עבד, cognate with the commentary's عبادت family, and locates worshipful service within a household declaration.

The commentary's explicit Beyt or house image corresponds formally to Hebrew bêt in 'house of the God of Jacob'; the verse's actual context supplies ascent and taught paths, not a lexical claim alone.

Arabic ism in بِسْمِ and Hebrew shem are cognate name terms; Deuteronomy uses shem for the divine name dwelling where offerings are brought, while the commentary's listed س م و label is not being treated as proof.

row.basis: Arabic م ل ك and Hebrew מלך
row.note: Hebrew melek, cognate with the source's مٰلِك family, means king here; Esther's actual transfer to the king's palace gives a concrete royal-marital setting without equating the two traditions' marriage vocabulary.
The lights serve for signs and appointed seasons; this is a specific biblical pairing for the commentary's marked season, though it is cosmic rather than pilgrimage law.
Israel camps by standards and signs of ancestral houses around the Tent; marked communal gathering around a dwelling gives a concrete analogue to the season-as-sign image.
The ark goes before Israel to seek out a resting place, a covenantal guide moving the people toward a place where they may settle.
God leads the returning people by streams on a straight path where they will not stumble; it gives a prophetic form of safe guidance, though the verse names no house.
Boaz says Ruth has come to seek refuge under YHWH's wings after leaving her own people; it is a personal migration into protected covenantal belonging.
The Targum renders Ruth's refuge as taking shelter under the wings of the Shekinah, making her foreign arrival an explicitly Jewish covenantal shelter image.
Abigail loads food gifts onto donkeys and takes them to David during a dangerous encounter; it is a carried gift aimed at a potentially hostile recipient.
Abigail calls the gift she has brought David a blessing, supplying a biblical way in which a conveyed present is spoken of as benefit.
Jacob asks Esau to accept his blessing, meaning the present sent ahead; a gift between estranged kin is thus expressed through blessing language.

row.basis: gift opens access to the great
row.note: A person's gift makes room for him and brings him before great people, a concise wisdom-text account of a gift as mediated access to a recipient.

row.basis: gift at altar and reconciled relation
row.note: Jesus' altar saying makes the acceptability of a gift depend on repairing a broken relation first, a relevant contrast to the commentary's distinction between gift to friend and to rival.
The prepared virgins go with the bridegroom into the wedding feast and the door is shut, portraying a completed movement into a wedding household.

row.basis: shepherd calls by name and leads sheep
row.note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out; animal, name, and guidance are joined, though the sheep are not sacrificial offerings.
Whoever enters through Jesus is saved and finds pasture; the doorway turns guidance into safety and sustenance rather than a Temple destination.
Zacharias says God's dawn will guide feet into the way of peace, a focused New Testament articulation of the prayer for guidance without the house image.
The shepherd comes home with the recovered sheep and calls friends and neighbors to rejoice; return, animal, home, and friendship meet in the parable.
The faithful seek a better, heavenly country, and God has prepared a city for them; pilgrimage toward a divinely prepared home is explicit.
Believers have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, expressing the destination as an already approached heavenly sanctuary.
Christians have no lasting city here but seek the city that is coming, a compact formulation of road-like yearning for final belonging.
Paul calls Christ the sacrificed Passover; read beside Exodus 12, it recasts the household-protecting sacrificial pattern through Christ rather than a Temple-bound animal.
Mary pours costly perfume on Jesus in a house, a concrete gift of devotion whose domestic setting and beloved recipient recall the commentary's gift image.

row.ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 67.2
row.basis: many dwellings in the Father's house
row.note: Augustine reads John 14's many dwellings as the differing places of blessedness in God's one house, making the destination more than a passing lodging.

row.basis: house of God and gate of heaven
row.note: Jacob calls Bethel the house of God and the gate of heaven; it gives the commentary's final home a threshold where earthly travel meets divine presence.
Jacob's vow asks God to be with him and guard him on the way he travels, a direct individual counterpart to a request for guidance with protection.

row.basis: return in peace to father's house
row.note: Jacob seeks to return safely to his father's house; the goal of the guarded road is explicitly a home and restored belonging.
The Bethel stone is to become God's house, and Jacob vows a tithe from what God gives him; sacred dwelling and conveyed gift are conjoined.

row.basis: go to Bethel, dwell, and build altar
row.note: God tells Jacob to arise, go to Bethel, dwell there, and make an altar; route, settlement, and sacrificial worship are inseparable instructions.
Jacob says God answered him in distress and was with him on the way, then calls his household to go build an altar at Bethel.
Jacob builds an altar at Bethel and names the place El-Bethel, making arrival at God's house culminate in sacrificial action.
YHWH goes before Israel in cloud and fire to lead them on the way, an explicit wilderness model for divine direction.
Following the holy-dwelling line, the song says God will bring and plant his people at the mountain of his inheritance, the place made for his dwelling and sanctuary.
God says he bore Israel on eagles' wings and brought them to himself; divine conveyance creates the covenantal nearness sought in the commentary.
God permits an altar for animal offerings and promises to come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; this directly joins sacrifice, name, and divine approach.
God promises that no one will covet Israel's land while its males go up for the three pilgrimage festivals; travel to worship is placed under explicit protection.

row.basis: first fruits brought to God's house
row.note: The first of the land's produce must be brought into the house of YHWH, a compact Torah model for a gift physically conveyed to the sacred home.
A voluntary herd burnt offering is brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting for acceptance before YHWH, giving a more formal sacrificial arrival scene.

row.basis: seeking the place of the Name
row.note: Israel is commanded to seek the place YHWH chooses for his name and dwelling; the verb of seeking makes pilgrimage toward the house explicit.

row.basis: journey too long to carry the gift
row.note: Deuteronomy considers the practical case in which the chosen place is too far for someone to carry the tithe, a precise biblical reflection on a religious gift in transit.
Firstborn animals from herd and flock are eaten before YHWH year by year at the chosen place, combining animal, pilgrimage, and household celebration.
The household rejoices at the place where YHWH causes his name to dwell together with Levite, resident alien, orphan, and widow; seasonal gathering includes vulnerable outsiders.

row.basis: basket of first fruits to chosen place
row.note: The worshiper takes first fruits in a basket and goes to the place YHWH chooses for his name; this is unusually close to the commentary's tray-borne gift.

row.basis: gift set before God and worshiped
row.note: The first fruits are brought and set before YHWH, followed by worship; gift delivery becomes an act of devotion at the sacred destination.
God promises to gather Israel even from the ends of heaven, a return movement for people who are dispersed and outside their secure place.
God brings the gathered people back into the land of their ancestors and makes them possess it, making return culminate in a home and inheritance.
Rahab and her family are spared and she dwells in Israel because of the oath-bound protection she gave the spies; asylum, covenant, and communal incorporation coincide.

row.basis: foreigner comes from afar for the Name
row.note: Solomon imagines a foreigner hearing of YHWH's great name and coming from a distant country, a pilgrimage of an outsider toward the named house.
God is asked to hear the foreigner who prays toward the Temple so all peoples know his name; house, name, and outsider access are explicitly related.
The congregation is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come before him; elevated name and conveyed offering share one command.

row.basis: house and altar of burnt offering
row.note: David identifies the future site as both God's house and the altar of burnt offering for Israel, an exact house-and-sacrifice formulation.
God's choice of Jerusalem for his name makes the temple city a named destination, supplementing the commentary's stress on a house reached through worship.

row.basis: right way for people and possessions
row.note: Ezra proclaims a fast to seek from God a right way for the returning people, their children, and their property, a concrete prayer for safeguarded travel.
God's hand delivers the returning caravan from enemy and ambush on the way, giving the safe-route element a historical narrative form.
The transported silver, gold, and vessels are weighed in the house of God at Jerusalem; a carried offering demonstrably reaches its sacred recipient.
Job says no stranger had to lodge in the street because he opened his doors to the traveler, a domestic counterpart to sheltering the one who arrives.

row.basis: homeless poor brought into one's house
row.note: Isaiah defines righteous care in part as bringing the homeless poor into one's house, an exact home-making act for a vulnerable outsider.
On God's holy mountain Israel will serve him and bring offerings, first fruits, and holy gifts; destination, service, and conveyed gift all appear in one verse.
God makes an everlasting covenant of peace, multiplies the people, and sets his sanctuary among them; covenant becomes enduring protected proximity.
God's dwelling is with the people, and he is their God while they are his people; the final home is reciprocal belonging.
Resident aliens who live among Israel and have children there receive inheritance among the tribes; protection reaches the level of a permanent home.
The prophet calls prisoners of hope to return to their stronghold, a compact return-to-safety image for threatened people.
Abel brings firstborn animals from his flock and their fat portions, and YHWH regards him and his offering; animal gift and acceptance are explicit.
Cain's offering is not regarded, providing another scriptural instance in which the relation between giver and recipient, rather than conveyance alone, determines an offering's reception.
Samuel says obedience and listening are better than sacrifice and rams' fat; this directly challenges any reading in which the guided animal itself exhausts worship.

row.basis: rejected offerings at a hated festival
row.note: God says he will not accept offerings or regard peace offerings in a prophetic critique of cult; it counterbalances the commentary's festival sacrifice with the ethical conditions of acceptance.
The worshiper is told to ascribe glory to YHWH's name, bring an offering, and come into his courts, a close formulaic counterpart to the commentary's named animal and house.
The speaker says the king has brought her into his chambers, a concise bridal arrival image in which the groom's dwelling is the destination.
The woman says she would lead her beloved into her mother's house; its reversed direction and household make it a useful contrary bride-and-home image.
Malachi calls the wife a partner and wife of covenant, giving a concise biblical equation of marriage with a binding protective relationship.

row.basis: blessing expressed in herds and camels
row.note: Abraham's blessing is narrated as flocks, herds, wealth, servants, camels, and donkeys; it illuminates the commentary's association of received benefit with herd animals and the bridal camel journey.
Jacob selects a gift for Esau before their feared meeting, an actual gift sent ahead to repair a dangerous relationship.

row.basis: gifts carried to a powerful unknown recipient
row.note: Jacob sends his sons with choice products as a present to the Egyptian ruler, a carried gift aimed at a recipient whose disposition is uncertain.
God says the priests place his name on Israel and he blesses them; the name functions as a bearer of benefit rather than merely an utterance over an animal.
Israel is to fear and serve YHWH and swear by his name; Hebrew עבד supplies a cognate service context alongside the commentary's name-and-worship connection.

row.basis: nations bring gifts to God's Name
row.note: Tobit's hymn foresees nations coming from afar with gifts in hand for the heavenly king because of the Lord's name, combining pilgrimage, gift, and exalted name.
An angel directs Joseph to take the child and mother and flee to Egypt from lethal danger, a New Testament journey of protected asylum.
Joseph takes the child and mother by night and withdraws to Egypt, giving the refugee movement itself its own narrative verse.
The angel tells Joseph to take the child and mother back to Israel because the threat has died; refuge ends in a guided return home.

row.basis: going out to meet the bridegroom
row.note: The virgins take lamps and go out to meet the bridegroom, supplying the journey-to-wedding aspect whose arrival is described later in the parable.
John calls the bride the bridegroom's and identifies the listening friend who rejoices at his voice; bride, husband, and friend are explicitly differentiated.
Jesus says he guarded his followers in the Father's name and none was lost except the designated exception; the name is presented as protective custody.

row.basis: relief gift for a distant community
row.note: The disciples determine to send relief to the brothers living in Judea, an actual communal gift conveyed to people in need.
The relief is sent to the elders through Barnabas and Saul, preserving the physical mediation of a gift's journey to its recipients.

row.basis: alms and offerings brought after travel
row.note: Paul says that after years away he came to bring alms for his nation and offerings, directly joining travel, gift, and cultic act.
Macedonia and Achaia make a contribution for poor saints in Jerusalem, a Christian gift carried toward a named communal home.
The author speaks of people who have fled for refuge to hold fast hope; an asylum image is used directly, even though its meaning is theological.
Hope enters the inner place behind the curtain, carrying the refuge image into access to God's sanctuary rather than a secular shelter.
The author praises faithful service to brothers who are strangers, a concrete Christian mandate to receive travelling outsiders.
The travelling brothers go out for the sake of the Name while taking nothing from outsiders, relating hospitality to named religious mission.
Angels are told not to harm land or sea until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads; a visible divine mark creates temporary inviolability.

row.basis: only the unsealed may be harmed
row.note: The destructive creatures may harm only those lacking God's seal on their foreheads, continuing the marked-protection pattern with an explicit exclusion.
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with people bearing his and his Father's name on their foreheads, binding Name, mark, and sacred destination.

row.basis: invited to the Lamb's marriage supper
row.note: The blessed are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb, giving the bridal arrival a communal table and final welcome.

row.basis: servants worship in the final city
row.note: In the renewed city God's servants worship him; permanent dwelling and service meet after the removal of the curse.
The servants see God's face and bear his name on their foreheads, completing the New Testament line of name as identity and protection.
After shipwreck, the islanders show unusual kindness and kindle a fire for all the survivors, a narrative of emergency welcome.

row.basis: shipwrecked travelers received into a house
row.note: Publius receives Paul and the shipwrecked party and entertains them for three days, an explicit house-based shelter for travellers.

This Mekhilta discussion is commonly cited as reading Exodus 15's holy dwelling and sanctuary in Temple terms; the exact wording and subdivision should be verified, but its interpretive bridge is sacrifice's destination as God's house.

row.basis: pilgrims form a common sacred homeland
row.note: Philo describes festival pilgrims leaving their local places for the Temple and recovering a common kinship there; the cited section should be checked, but it is a specific Hellenistic-Jewish expansion of travel into sacred home.

row.basis: God leads the restored people with joy
row.note: Baruch says God will lead Israel in joy by the light of his glory with mercy and righteousness; its restoration context supplies a later Jewish guided-homecoming image.
After finding the sheep, the shepherd puts it on his shoulders rejoicing; this is the carrying action that culminates in the homecoming already represented by the next verse.

row.basis: prisoners welcomed into the jailer's house
row.note: The jailer brings Paul and Silas into his house and sets food before them after their release, converting a scene of custody and fear into domestic welcome.

row.basis: receive a contested person as oneself
row.note: Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul; without assuming Onesimus's legal status, the verse makes personal welcome the requested resolution.
Christ's death mediates a new covenant so those called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, relating sacrifice to secure belonging rather than an animal's arrival.
